## Hard-to-vary report: Hume, Section VII ("Of the Idea of Necessary Connexion")

**1. The question, frozen.** The title and the opening lines fix it: *what is the idea of power, force, energy, necessary connexion, and from what impression is it copied?* Range: every idea, in every kind of case where one might come from — bodies on bodies (the billiard balls, flame and heat), mind on body (the will moving a limb), mind on itself (the will raising an idea) — plus the step from one instance to many. Kind: mostly backward ("what can we tell from what we see?"), with a nested absence question ("why is there no impression of the tie?"). Held still throughout.

**2. The parts, in his words.**
A. Copy principle: every idea is a copy of an impression; no impression, no idea.
B. In single instances we observe only succession: the ball's impulse is "attended with" motion; "this is the whole that appears to the outward senses."
C. No sensible quality — solidity, extension, motion — "points out any other event."
D. Will over body: no felt power; the palsy case; anatomy's hidden chain of muscles, nerves, animal spirits.
E. Will over ideas: a "real creation"; the limits; strength varies with health, hour, fasting.
F. Many uniform instances produce a "customary transition of the imagination"; the connexion we *feel* is the impression the idea is copied from.
G. Two definitions of cause: constant conjunction; the mind's transition.
H. The occasionalist rival (God's volitions do the work; bodies are only occasions) and its rejection.

**3. Part by part.**

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A | **Borrowed** | Rests on Section II's proof; not tested here. |
| B | **Held** | Swap the example (billiard → flame → falling bodies) and it says the same. Every instance tried holds it. |
| C | **Held** | Same job from the other side: a quality's sensible surface never points onward. |
| D | **Two routes** | The palsy case and the anatomy each do the limb job alone. Neither is needed singly. |
| E | **Held** | The limits and their variation are the job; blocked until someone assigns the limits by reason. |
| F | **Held if** | Held only by the job "there really is a felt being-carried from one idea to the next." That job is in doubt: the feeling is partly read off the very inference it is meant to explain. Settled by an independent grip on the transition. |
| G | **Held** | Both definitions are relational because nothing in the cause can be pointed at. |
| H | **Idle** for the central question — remove it and the account of the idea is untouched. It works only for a job I added: "reject the occasionalist rival." Flagged as mine. |

Also "secret mechanism or structure of parts" and "something still more minute and more unknown" (¶53): a **catch-all**, with anatomy as a partial gauge — anatomy does find real intermediate links.

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**

*Flip.* Had a single instance shown the tie, the account collapses — it says so. Had we never come to expect the usual attendant, it also collapses. It sticks its neck out both ways. The weak joint: F is built so the second cannot happen, since the felt transition just *is* the reading of the belief.

*Direction.* Mostly forward-poked: raise the count of uniform instances and the belief moves; change the objects and it does not. But F is partly read backwards off the result.

*Answer hidden in the starting points?* "Custom, habit, customary transition" is close to a restatement of "we make the inference" wearing an impression's clothes. Not fully circular — F adds a claim beyond the belief, that the feeling is introspectively available and grows with repetition — but the closeness is the thing to watch.

*The jobs, and where they came from.* J1 (why "connected" and not merely "conjoined"), J2 (why we cannot foresee without experience), J3 (why the will moves tongue and fingers, not heart or liver), J4 (why the paralysed man feels the same power), J5 (why repetition changes anything) — all **given** by the text. The copy principle is a **fixed** premise imported, not tested here.

*Pairs that pull.* A (no impression, no idea) against G (cause defined by "circumstances foreign to it"). The harder A bites, the worse it looks that the central term is defined relationally and never by an impression — Hume concedes the inconvenience. Which gives way: the definition of cause. What would show the line was drawn wrongly: someone producing the impression of the tie. Separately, B against F: the harder the claim that no tie is observable in objects, the less the felt tie can be a perception rather than an inference. Giveway: the objective tie.

*Catch-alls and gauges.* "Secret mechanism" carries a partial gauge. The rival "real but insensible powers" carries none — which is why B kills it. The same charge can be turned on F.

*What the change list leaves out.* Whether the idea could be innate; animals and infants (handled elsewhere); whether the conjunction is real in the world — openly disclaimed up front ("we may fix the meaning," not the metaphysics). All left out in the open, so no fault.

*Best rival.* Occasionalism. Distinguishing change: put a man before two colliding balls who has never seen the like. Hume's account says he feels no connexion; the occasionalist says the connexion (God's decree) is there regardless. That change separates them, and it favours Hume's account. But H is **borrowed**: it rests on a theory of how God operates which Hume himself says we understand no better than anything else.

*Where each part came from.* A **borrowed**; B, C, E **asserted** (introspective reports others cannot check); D's "animal spirits" **fitted** to the physiology of the day — which is why D needs the palsy route, since that route survives a change of physiology; F **built** with a fitted tail; G **built**; H **borrowed**.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** One: an independent grip on the felt transition — a case where the conjunction is complete but the feeling is absent, or the reverse. Two: an impression of the tie in a single instance. Either tightens F sharply or breaks it cleanly.

**6. What this does not show.** A hard-to-vary explanation is not a true one. This account could be tight at every joint and still wrong about the world.

**7. One next step.** Run the newcomer poke: show a man who has never seen an impulse, and ask both this account and its occasionalist rival what he feels and what is true.
